strengths: Provides an interesting and relatively underexplored perspective connecting gated linear units (GLUs) to frequency-domain behavior in neural network training, motivated by the convolution theorem and differential properties of the Fourier transform.

Extensive empirical validation across multiple backbones (ResNet18, MobileNetV2, EfficientFormer-v2) and multiple frequency thresholds, showing a consistent qualitative pattern that GLUs with non-smooth activations (ReLU6) improve high-frequency classification while smooth activations (GELU) favor low-frequency components.

The proposed lightweight model GmNet achieves a competitive accuracy-latency trade-off on ImageNet-1K compared to many recent efficient architectures (RepViT, StarNet, MobileOne, EfficientFormer variants), without relying on re-parameterization or knowledge distillation.
Reasonably thorough ablation studies on GLU variants (LN, DW, pooling-based) and activation function choices, connecting the design choices back to the frequency analysis framework.
Additional bandwidth analysis of learned convolution kernels offers a complementary, if informal, piece of evidence supporting the frequency-domain narrative.
weaknesses: The core theoretical contributions (Theorem 1: convolution theorem; Theorem 2/Lemma 3: differentiability-decay relationship for Fourier transforms) are standard, well-known mathematical facts rather than novel results specific to this work; the paper largely restates textbook signal-processing theory rather than deriving new theoretical insight into gating mechanisms per se.

The connection between the abstract theoretical statements (e.g., self-convolution broadens frequency support) and the concrete claims about deep, multi-layer, nonlinear networks trained on real images is asserted rather than rigorously established; no formal analysis bridges the simple 1D theoretical setting to the actual multi-channel, multi-layer GmNet architecture.

The frequency-band classification methodology (accuracy on low-/high-pass filtered images) is adopted from prior work ([11]) without deeper methodological scrutiny of confounds (e.g., filtering artifacts, loss of semantic content at high thresholds could trivially reduce accuracy regardless of gating).

Overall novelty of the proposed architecture is limited: GmNet is essentially a lightweight block with an added simple GLU (σ(x)·x) plus depthwise convolutions, which is an incremental architectural combination rather than a fundamentally new design; the frequency framing motivates but does not uniquely necessitate this specific architecture.

Fairness of the SOTA comparison in Table 2 is not fully clear — baseline methods may have been trained with different data augmentation/regularization recipes, and the paper does not verify that all baselines are trained under identical conditions (300 epochs, same optimizer, same augmentations); this could bias the accuracy-latency comparison.

No standard deviation or confidence intervals are reported for the main ImageNet comparison table (Table 2) despite variance being reported for the smaller-scale frequency experiments (Fig. 3, Table 3), weakening statistical confidence in headline accuracy numbers.

Manuscript has notable clarity and proofreading issues: incomplete/garbled sentences (e.g., ablation description cut off with 'range/'), inconsistent terminology ('modals' instead of 'models', 'continues' instead of 'continuous', 'interact' instead of 'interaction'), which detract from readability and suggest insufficient polishing.

Key evaluations beyond ImageNet classification (object detection, segmentation) are deferred entirely to supplementary material, limiting the strength of generality claims for GmNet in the main paper.

The bandwidth analysis of convolution kernels (Fig. 7) lacks a precise definition/description of how 'bandwidth' is computed in the main text, making this evidence difficult to independently verify or reproduce.

The paper's Limitations section acknowledges that GLUs may not generalize as a universal solution for larger/more complex architectures, which somewhat undercuts the broader significance of the theoretical framework beyond the specific lightweight-model regime studied.

strengths: The paper offers a fresh and coherent frequency-domain lens for analyzing gating mechanisms, combining convolution-theorem-based reasoning about element-wise products with Fourier differentiation properties of activation functions, providing an intuitive explanation for why GLUs help exploit high-frequency information.

The theoretical claims are backed by consistent empirical validation across three distinct architectures (ResNet18, MobileNetV2, EfficientFormer-v2), showing that adding GLUs (especially with non-smooth activations like ReLU6) improves high-frequency component classification, which strengthens the credibility of the frequency-based narrative.

The proposed GmNet achieves a strong accuracy-latency trade-off relative to many recent lightweight baselines (StarNet, RepViT, MobileOne, EfficientFormerV2, etc.) without relying on advanced training tricks such as distillation or re-parameterization, which is a meaningful practical contribution for efficient model design.

Thorough ablation studies (activation function choice, GLU design variants, bandwidth analysis of convolution kernels) provide multiple angles of evidence supporting the core hypothesis and design choices of GmNet.
The paper explicitly discusses limitations and scope (e.g., that GLU benefits may diminish in larger/more complex architectures), showing self-awareness about the generality of the claims.
weaknesses: The 'theoretical' results (Theorem 1 on convolution theorem, Theorem 2/Lemma 3 on Fourier differentiation) are standard textbook facts rather than novel derivations; the paper's real theoretical contribution is the qualitative interpretive framework connecting these facts to gating behavior, which is more heuristic than rigorous, and the leap from these general facts to concrete architectural decisions (e.g., using ReLU6, specific kernel sizes) is not formally justified.

The frequency decomposition methodology (threshold-based radius r on 2D DFT) is somewhat coarse, and the paper does not fully justify why this particular way of splitting frequencies is the right proxy for 'information content that matters for classification,' especially given that very high-frequency components are described as 'nearly imperceptible to the human eye' yet used to draw strong conclusions.

Several quantitative claims and thresholds appear ad hoc (e.g., 'an improvement which is remarkable should exceed 1.0' in Table 5), without statistical significance testing or reported variance/error bars in the main accuracy tables (Table 2, Table 4), despite averaging over multiple runs elsewhere.

Downstream task results (detection, segmentation) that would validate the generality of the approach beyond ImageNet classification are relegated entirely to supplementary material and not discussed in the main text, weakening the significance claims made in the abstract/intro about broad applicability.

Architectural novelty is modest: GmNet is largely a conventional hybrid conv/GLU block design integrated into an existing MobileNet-style macro-architecture, and comparisons, while favorable, are against a mix of older and moderately recent baselines rather than the most current state-of-the-art efficient architectures.

Code is not released at submission time (promised only upon acceptance), limiting immediate reproducibility, and some writing/typographical issues (e.g., 'interact,' 'modals,' inconsistent phrasing) detract from overall polish.

strengths: Novel angle connecting GLU/gating mechanisms to spectral bias, linking convolution theorem (element-wise multiplication <-> frequency convolution) and activation-function smoothness (Fourier decay rate) to a network's ability to learn high-frequency information.

Extensive empirical validation across multiple backbones (ResNet-18, MobileNetV2, EfficientFormer-V2, ConvNeXt) and multiple frequency thresholds, showing a consistent pattern that non-smooth activations (ReLU/ReLU6) improve high-frequency component classification while smooth activations (GELU/SiLU) favor low-frequency components.

Strong practical results: the proposed GmNet architecture achieves a favorable accuracy-latency trade-off compared to many recent efficient models (StarNet, RepViT, EfficientFormer, MobileOne, etc.) on ImageNet-1K without relying on re-parameterization, distillation, or NAS.
Thorough ablation studies on GLU variants (LN, DW, Pool, FC-based), activation choices, and a 'contribution breakdown' table isolating the effect of the gating unit under matched FLOPs/params.

Additional supporting evidence via convolution kernel bandwidth analysis and quantitative high/low frequency energy ratios, and validation on downstream tasks (detection, instance segmentation, semantic segmentation) and a secondary dataset (CUB-100).
weaknesses: The theoretical justification is somewhat informal: the convolution theorem argument is illustrated only for idealized global self-convolution of a 1D signal and does not rigorously establish how local, learned, per-channel element-wise products embedded within a deep nonlinear network actually broaden the effective frequency spectrum of the representation. The activation-smoothness argument (Fourier decay rates) is a well-known general fact, applied here somewhat heuristically to features after several nonlinear conv layers, without a rigorous derivation connecting it to end-to-end classification accuracy.

The core diagnostic methodology (training/evaluating classifiers on radially frequency-masked images to gauge 'high/low-frequency learning ability') is a proxy metric whose relationship to a model's true internal spectral bias is not firmly established; results appear sensitive to the choice of cutoff radius r (as acknowledged in the appendix), raising concerns about robustness/cherry-picking of the reported r values in the main text.

The novelty claim of being the 'first systematic analysis of GLUs from a frequency perspective' is somewhat overstated given that the underlying Fourier facts (convolution theorem, smoothness-decay relationship, spectral bias) are all well-established in prior work; the paper's contribution is largely an application/combination of known principles rather than new theory.

Presentation and polish issues: the abstract is truncated ('Our code can be found in'), and the appendix contains artifacts suggesting rebuttal content was pasted in without proper editing (e.g., 'Following the reviewer's advice...', a broken citation '?' in Section A.7), which raises concerns about the manuscript's finalization and quality control.

Comparisons are restricted to other lightweight/efficient models; there is limited discussion of how the proposed frequency-aware gating principle would scale to larger models or interact with more advanced training recipes (though a ConvNeXt experiment is included, gains there are much smaller, which is only briefly explained).

Robustness discussion (PGD accuracy comparison) is very limited (one dataset, two activation variants, small delta), insufficient to strongly support the claimed accuracy-robustness trade-off framing highlighted as a motivating issue in the introduction.
